chapter: Chicago, Detroit and Seattle Harmony Kings
title: The Omer Hicks band, Roseland, and the Ross Gorman job the union blocked
summary: Chubb-Steinberg becomes the Omer Hicks band and tours East; at Roseland he meets Red Nichols and Miff Mole and is offered Gorman's chair but cannot join the New York union.

story.theme_name: The musicians' union: cards, locals, and the Black-white merger
story.community_name: The musicians' union: cards, scale and the black-white merger

blocks.x: Well, now, I think for the sake of speeding along here - I'm going to just - real quickly - you stop me if I--- if you want to throw something in --- but, uh, after a couple of years there with Chubb Steinberg that band broke up and it became Omer Hicks---
Yes.
---and you went on the road and you went around several parts of the Midwest and you went East and you played in New York at the Roseland Ballroom---
Yes.
---and you played for the Earl Carroll Bathtub Party --
Yeah - well, that's all going on here so---
Yeah and then you went on down and played in Baltimore and, finally, in Philadelphia and you finally left that Omar-Hicks Band and went back out to Defiance and tell about that - now, you started---
Well, I left the band--- I left that band--- well, what happened to the band --Chubb Steinberg---
there was trouble between the leader and Chubb. They couldn't see eye to eye so, uh, (Art) Hicks quit.
Right.
And, so, he was our leader and ---
Most of you went with him---
Well, sure because he had some work going through at that time an agent, I think, and, uh, he put on a different saxophone player-on the tenor, there was a guy named P.T.---
Omer---

Omer -- and, at that time, became the Omer Hicks band. I think that P.T. who later became a big lawyer in New York, is some place, had some money to sort of put into this thing. And, I left the band in Baltimore. I had worked the Roseland Ballroom and all those things and the Bathtub Party and all that stuff and we did a couple of jobs before - after we'd left and I had a chance to go with the, well, I met all those guys like when we were at the Roseland -- I met such guys as Red Nichols and Miff Mole and all of those guys and, uh, they--- we were opposite Fletcher Henderson at that time in the Roseland and there used to be a little speak-easy half way between the Roseland and the bottom floor and the bottom floor - there was a place where Ross Gorman had a band - you know - and, uh, Miff Mole and Red Nichols were with Gorman and, uh, Red was leaving the band

and Red told Ross Gorman that maybe he ought to go up and hear me play. And, maybe I could take his place. And, so, Ross Gorman said -- do you think you could handle it - and I said, well, with my reading - if you let me take the parts and take them home -- he said, well, that can be arranged---
At that time, to read stuff - you had to study it - right?
Oh, boy, yes - because I was a terrible reader at that time and, so, he decided he'd let me have a chance at it. But, what he didn't know is that the union wouldn't let me in.
Oh.
---and I went over to the union -- they said - almost as much as - get out of town -- so, I didn't quit the band; I stayed until Baltimore.
